sections.body: Backup storage strategy starts with the data's criticality, recovery point, confidentiality, integrity, retention, geographic risk, dependency, and restoration capacity. Onsite copies may restore quickly but share a site failure; offsite or cloud copies improve geographic separation but add network, provider, identity, and key dependencies. Define the copy schedule, consistency model, encryption, access path, immutability or deletion protection, restore owner, and evidence that the copy is usable. RPO is an outcome requirement, not a promise created by naming a backup tier.
keyPoints: Location and independence matter as much as backup frequency.
A protected copy is not useful if keys, credentials, bandwidth, or compatible software are unavailable.
Recovery evidence should show both copy currency and successful restoration.
sections.title: Match storage to data-loss tolerance

sections.body: A cold site provides space and basic facilities with more build time; a warm site provides some prepared capacity; a hot site or multiple processing site can reduce interruption but requires synchronized data, identity, network, keys, staffing, licensing, and operational acceptance. Reciprocal arrangements depend on compatible assumptions and a partner's availability during the same event. Compare the time and capacity to restore the complete service, not merely the application. Include regional, provider, supplier, environmental, and common-mode failure in the decision.
keyPoints: Site readiness is a spectrum of capability, not a binary available/unavailable label.
Multiple sites can share the same software, identity, provider, or human dependency.
Capacity agreements must be tested under concurrent demand and declared-event conditions.
